title: Displacing misinformation about events: An experimental test of causal corrections

source.title: Displacing misinformation about events: An experimental test of causal corrections
source.venue: Journal of Experimental Political Science (forthcoming at the time of the supplement)

studies.title: Swensen resignation dispatches experiment (YouGov survey, Oct 13-16, 2012)
studies.description: A four-condition, block-randomized online survey experiment in which respondents read dispatches about a fictional Alaska state senator's resignation (control, innuendo, denial, causal correction) and then rated his favorability and the likelihood he took bribes / resigned because of an investigation. The paper reports this one experiment.

evidence.quote: We test this hypothesis using an experimental paradigm adapted from the psychology literature on the continued influence effect and find that a causal explanation for an unexplained event is significantly more effective than a denial even when the denial is backed by unusually strong evidence.
false information may continue to influence beliefs and attitudes even after being debunked if it is not replaced by an alternate causal explanation.
As a result, false information may persist and continue to influence judgments even after it has been debunked if it is not displaced by an alternate causal account.

In the canonical paradigm in the continued influence effect literature (Wilkes and Leatherbarrow 1988), subjects are told one piece of information at a time about an unfolding fictional event (typically, a fire in a warehouse).

Johnson and Seifert (1994) build on the findings of Wilkes and Leatherbarrow (1988) by showing that the incorrect link between flammable chemicals and the fire can be displaced when an alternative cause (arson) is provided for the fire – a finding that was replicated by Ecker, Lewandowsky, and Apai in a plane crash scenario (2011).

Specifically, we examine how a particular type of information (a causal correction) can help prevent new misperceptions from taking root in the context of a realistic fast-breaking political news story that includes speculative and unconfirmed reports.
The breaking news event in our experiment is the sudden and unexpected resignation of a politician.

More importantly, we show that even providing evidence against the innuendo is not enough to undo its damage to respondents’ views of the politician. By contrast, adding an alternate causal explanation for why the politician resigned is significantly more effective in limiting acceptance of misperceptions
YouGov collected data for this study from October 13-16, 2012 as part of the 2012 Cooperative
Respondents were matched and weighted to population targets using the firm’s sample matching procedure, which is designed to approximate a nationally representative sample (Rivers N.d.).

The demographic characteristics of the 1000 respondents in our final sample are thus approximately representative of the U.S. population (details available upon request). In particular, 35% identified as Democrats and 27% as Republicans.

Participants in our study read a series of short news items, which we call “dispatches,” about a fictional state senator in Alaska named Don Swensen. They were randomly assigned to one of four conditions that differed in the number and content of dispatches read. Only one dispatch was displayed on the screen at a time.
respondents were block-randomized to each condition based on their response to an American National Election Studies question about the extent to which “the people running the government” are crooked

Given that our study concerned innuendo about political misconduct, we used this procedure to ensure that our sample was balanced on prior beliefs about the prevalence of unethical behavior among public officials rather than relying on random assignment alone
This question was asked before the experiment so that it could be used as a pre-treatment moderator in the subsequent analysis.

Table 1 presents the exact wording of the dispatches that subjects received in each condition. Each dispatch included the date and time of their ostensible publication and was presented on a separate page for respondents to read. After respondents read a dispatch, they proceeded sequentially to the next one (moving downward in the table), continuing in chronological order until they completed the dispatches available in their condition.

The distributions of several key demographic characteristics across experimental conditions are presented in the online appendix. None of the distributions are significantly different from what we would expect due to chance, suggesting that the randomization was successful.
In the control condition, subjects received information that Swensen resigned from office without any indication why he resigned.
In the innuendo condition, subjects received news of the resignation as well as information suggesting that Swensen resigned because of a bribery investigation.

The denial condition is the same as the innuendo condition except that it also includes a dispatch in which Swensen denies the bribery allegation and provides a letter from prosecutors stating that he is not under investigation
Finally, the causal correction condition is the same as the denial except that it includes an additional dispatch providing an alternate explanation for his resignation

The causal correction was provided in addition to the denial rather than in place of it in order to test whether it was more effective than a denial alone. While this design choice means that the dispatch participants read in the causal condition was two sentences longer than the denial condition
In the context of the study, the claim that Swensen resigned due to an investigation is never definitively disproved
Future research should also consider whether these effects vary depending on the valence of the causal explanation.
After completing unscramble and word search tasks intended to clear working memory, we asked respondents to report their beliefs and attitudes toward Swensen on two outcome measures.

Respondents in each condition were asked their opinion of Swensen on a six-point scale from “very unfavorable (1) to “very favorable” (6) and whether they believe it is likely that he “accepted bribes or engaged in other illegal practices” on a five-point scale from “not at all likely” (1) to “extremely likely” (5).
In addition, respondents who were exposed to the innuendo (i.e., not assigned to the control condition) were also asked how likely they think it is that he
resigning from office because he is under investigation for bribery” on a four-point scale from “not likely at all” (1) to “very likely” (4).
Table 2 presents OLS models estimating the effect of the innuendo, denial, and causal correction treatments on respondents’ opinion of Swensen and their beliefs about he took bribes or broke the law.

We also estimate the effect of the denial and causal correction treatments on respondents’ belief that Swensen resigned due to the investigation. Because this question was only asked of respondents who were exposed to the rumor about his resignation, respondents in the innuendo condition serve as controls in these models.

As the table indicates, each model was estimated using both inverse probability weights accounting for varying probabilities of treatment due to block randomization (Gerber and Green 2012: 117) and YouGov survey weights intended to help ensure that the data approximate a national probability sample.
The results are substantively identical if we estimate the models using ordered probit
Estimated treatment effects are substantively identical when the models are estimated without weights of any kind
exposure to innuendo significantly reduced how favorably respondents viewed Swensen (-.58 and -.52, respectively; p<.01). The denial failed to completely repair the damage.

Despite being told of credible evidence against the innuendo (a letter from prosecutors stating he is not under investigation), respondents still viewed Swensen significantly less favorably than controls (-.39 and -.41, p<.01).
the causal correction significantly increased favorability relative to respondents in the innuendo condition (.66, p<.01 using results from Model 1; .32, p<.05 using Model 2).

The marginal effect of the denial relative to the innuendo was significant at the p<.10 level using inverse probability weights (Model 1) but not using survey weights (Model 2).

When compared directly, respondents in the causal correction condition viewed Swensen significantly more favorably than those in the denial condition using inverse probability weights (p<.01) but the difference was not quite significant using survey weights (p<.12).
We again find significant damage incurred by the innuendo, which in this case makes respondents much more likely to believe Swensen engaged in illegal activity (.78 and .67, respectively; p<.01).
Respondents who received Swensen’s denial were still more likely than controls to believe he had broken the law (.55 and .52, p<.01).

significantly reducing belief that Swensen took bribes or committed other crimes relative to the innuendo (-.72 and -.51 using results from Models 3 and 4, respectively; p<.01) and denial (-.48, p<.01 using results from Model 3; -.36, p<.05 using Model 4).
We thus cannot reject the null hypothesis of no difference in belief in Swensen breaking the law between the control and causal correction conditions.

Specifically, we cannot reject the null hypothesis of no difference in response accuracy on a three-question battery between the innuendo, denial, and causal correction conditions (results are provided in the online appendix).

The marginal effect of the denial relative to the innuendo on beliefs about illegal activity was significant at the p<.05 level using inverse probability weights (Model 3) but not survey weights (Model 4).

Both Model 5 and Model 6 indicate that the denial and causal correction treatments significantly reduced belief in the bribery rumor (denial: -.25 and -.26, respectively, p<.01; causal correction: -.58 and -.42, p<.01).
did not quite reach significance in the survey weights model (-.34, p<.01 using results from Model 5; -.16, p<.12 using Model 6).
In particular, a denial failed to fully undo the damage to the fictional politician’s reputation caused by exposure to innuendo despite being backed by evidence (the letter from prosecutors).

By providing another explanation for the event in question (the resignation), the causal correction was able to reverse the damage from the innuendo, suggesting that it was necessary to displace the original attribution of the event to the investigation with an alternate account.
First, our results demonstrate that findings from the psychology literature on the continued influence effect apply to politics.

Second, we successfully adapt the paradigm of a sequence of short dispatches from the psychology literature on the continued influence effect to the political domain, mimicking the flow of information about breaking news, which frequently contains incorrect claims that are later corrected.

Finally, the study employs a novel breaking news paradigm in which the innuendo is never definitely disproved.
Future research should seek to determine if these results hold when partisanship or ideological factors are incorporated into the experiment.
the extent to which the findings of the study generalize is unknown.
BREAKING NEWS: State Senator Don Swensen, who represents part of the city of Juneau, has issued a brief press release stating that he has resigned from office.
Swensen is refusing further comment. Reporters are contacting Republican and Democratic leaders to see if they know why he resigned.

Spokespeople for both parties have said they have not been told why Swensen is leaving office, but rumors are circulating that his resignation is linked to yesterday's indictment of Robert Landry, a local developer, for embezzlement and tax fraud. Landry is one of the largest campaign donors to Swensen, who is legendary for his prodigious fundraising.
Speculation continues to grow among state legislative insiders about why Swensen left office so abruptly. Until today, the state senator was widely seen as a future candidate for governor.
With Swensen leaving office, a special election will be held to fill his seat in less than four weeks. Reports indicate that several potential candidates are already exploring a run.
Unconfirmed reports are circulating online that Landry is cooperating with prosecutors and may have implicated Swensen in a bribery scandal. Reporters are now investigating.
Senator Swensen’s seat is empty as the prestigious Finance Committee is called to order. A fierce battle to succeed him is likely to ensue.
Reporters are waiting outside Swensen’s home and state capitol office but have not been able to speak to him.
Members of Swensen’s legislative staff have been seen packing their boxes in his office at the state capital. One was seen shredding a series of documents.

Senator Swensen just held a press conference on his front porch denying the rumor that he was resigning because he is under investigation for bribery. He said he was leaving office for personal reasons and provided a letter from prosecutors stating that he has not been charged with any crime and is not under investigation.

Senator Swensen just held a press conference on his front porch denying the rumor that he was resigning because he is under investigation for bribery. He said he was leaving office for personal reasons and provided a letter from prosecutors stating that he has not been charged with any crime and is not under investigation. While the resignation seemed sudden, Swensen said that it has been in the works for some time. He was hired as the incoming president of the University of Alaska Southeast several weeks ago, he said, but could not disclose that information until this afternoon when the current president announced that he was stepping down.
Reporters have been informed that Senator Swensen has left the area with his family and will not provide further comment on his resignation.

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Between-subjects survey experiment (four conditions, block-randomized) fielded online by YouGov

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Respondents read a sequence of news dispatches about a fictional Alaska state senator's sudden resignation. Conditions differed in whether the resignation was left unexplained (control), linked by innuendo to a bribery investigation, followed by a denial backed by a prosecutors' letter, or followed by the denial plus an alternate causal explanation (a new job). After a delay task, respondents rated the senator's favorability and the likelihood of bribery or illegal practices (and, outside the control condition, of resigning because of an investigation).

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Whether a causal explanation for an unexplained event corrects a false (innuendo) account better than a denial alone, for new political misperceptions about a breaking news event.

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: Prior political-misinformation work mostly examines misperceptions already widely held; this study examines new misperceptions as they form, in a fast-breaking political news story with speculative and unconfirmed reports.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: People automatically make causal inferences from the information at hand; false information can persist after being debunked unless it is displaced by an alternate causal account (continued influence effect).

fields.label: Concepts
fields.value: Continued influence effect, belief perseverance, innuendo, denial, causal correction. In the canonical paradigm (Wilkes and Leatherbarrow 1988) subjects are told one piece of information at a time about an unfolding fictional event; Johnson and Seifert (1994) showed the false link can be displaced by an alternative cause.

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: False information may continue to influence beliefs and attitudes even after being debunked if it is not replaced by an alternate causal explanation; a causal explanation for an unexplained event should therefore be more effective than a denial, even a denial backed by strong evidence.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: A single fictional breaking-news event (a politician's sudden resignation) in which the innuendo is never definitively disproved.

fields.label: Setting
fields.value: Online survey fielded by YouGov, October 13-16, 2012, as part of the 2012 Cooperative Campaign Analysis Project; a single online session per respondent.

fields.label: Roles
fields.value: Respondent in one of four conditions; no confederates or other roles are described.

fields.label: Recruitment
fields.value: Respondents were matched and weighted to population targets using YouGov's sample matching procedure, designed to approximate a nationally representative sample.

fields.label: Final sample
fields.value: 1000 respondents in the final sample.

fields.label: Completed
fields.value: Data were provided by YouGov for 1000 respondents who completed the study; no known attrition.

fields.label: Analysed
fields.value: Models 1-2 (favorability) N = 987; Models 3-4 (bribes) N = 986; Models 5-6 (investigation) N = 764. Listwise deletion removed 13, 14 and 5 cases respectively; the investigation question was not asked of 231 control respondents.

fields.label: Characteristics
fields.value: Approximately representative of the U.S. population; 35% identified as Democrats and 27% as Republicans. Unweighted gender, education, race/ethnicity and age by condition are in the appendix balance table.

fields.label: Sampling unit
fields.value: Individual respondent (individual-level randomization and analysis).

fields.label: Compensation
fields.value: YouGov's normal survey participation incentives; no additional incentives.

fields.label: Attrition
fields.value: No known attrition.

fields.label: Type
fields.value: Between-subjects; four conditions that differ in the number and content of dispatches read; one dispatch per screen.

fields.label: Control
fields.value: Control condition: resignation with no indication why he resigned.

fields.label: Assignment
fields.value: Respondents were randomly assigned, block-randomized on their answer to an ANES question about how many people running the government are crooked, to improve precision and balance prior beliefs about official misconduct. Assignment was generated by the YouGov survey platform.

fields.label: Blocks
fields.value: Blocks are taken to be the four response options of the pre-treatment 'crooked' question.
fields.derivation: The paper says respondents were block-randomized on their response to this question; the appendix lists four response options; the paper does not state the blocks explicitly.

fields.label: Order
fields.value: Dispatches were read one per page in chronological order, moving downward in Table 1, within each respondent's condition; the pre-treatment question comes first, the delay tasks then the outcome questions come after the dispatches.

fields.label: Blinding
fields.value: Subjects were blind to which condition they were in.

fields.label: Manipulation check
fields.value: None reported as such. A three-question recall battery was used to check that effects were not due to differing recall of the event.

fields.label: Pre-specification
fields.value: All outcomes and conditions were specified before the study (only DVs and experimental conditions tested); no registration reported.

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Test
fields.value: Demographic distributions (gender, education, race/ethnicity, age) are not different from chance, unweighted or with survey weights; the test is not possible with IPW.

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: A denial failed to fully undo the damage of innuendo, while adding a causal explanation reversed it: causal-correction respondents were not distinguishable from control on favorability or belief in illegal activity.

fields.label: Support
fields.value: Table 2 Models 1-6 and the appendix pairwise comparisons.

fields.label: Mechanism proposed
fields.value: It was necessary to displace the original attribution of the event to the investigation with an alternate account.

fields.label: Contribution
fields.value: Findings from the continued influence literature apply to politics; the dispatch paradigm is adapted to breaking political news; citizens are easily influenced by innuendo.

fields.label: Validity
fields.value: Even in the causal correction condition respondents on average thought it 'somewhat likely' that he resigned due to a bribery investigation; the innuendo is never definitively disproved, so the claim cannot be ruled out with certainty.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Generalization is unknown beyond this fictional event and design; partisanship and ideology are not incorporated.

fields.label: Design limitations
fields.value: The causal dispatch was two sentences longer than the denial dispatch by design; the new job may itself affect favorability (valence of the causal explanation).

fields.label: Replications
fields.value: The paper cites Ecker, Lewandowsky and Apai (2011) as replicating Johnson and Seifert (1994) in a plane crash scenario; it reports no replication of its own.

fields.label: Openness
fields.value: Replication data to be posted on the first author's website after publication; the paper reports the experiment was reviewed by an IRB.

fields.label: Steps
fields.value: Possible: pre-treatment question, scenario introduction, the condition's dispatches one at a time, and the outcome questions, all as printed. Excluded: the unscramble and word search delay tasks (content not printed) and the recall questions (position in the survey not stated).

fields.label: Roles
fields.value: Every original participant is an AI participant; the paper has no confederates or scripted roles. Dispatch text is pre-written stimulus, shown as printed.

fields.label: Conditions
fields.value: All four conditions can be run with the printed dispatches. Block randomization on the pre-treatment question is replaced by running an equal number of AI participants per condition; survey weights and inverse probability weights cannot be reproduced.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: Favorability, belief in bribery, and (outside control) belief in the investigation rumor can be collected on the printed scales and compared with Table 2 and the appendix means. Recall is not collected.

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: An AI participant has no working-memory interference, no real news habits and no demographic or political background unless one is added; results are a simulation, not observations of people, and agreement with the paper would not show that people behave the same way. The survey weights, sample demographics and panel are not reproduced.

rule.label: Position of the recall questions in the survey sequence

issues.title: Delay task content is not given
issues.reason: The paper says respondents completed unscramble and word search tasks to clear working memory; the appendix shows only a placeholder for the delay content. Neither task items nor duration are stated.
issues.impact: The replay cannot reproduce the delay. AI participants answer from the dispatches without the interference of the tasks, which may change recall and attitude judgments.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the task content and duration if known; otherwise keep the replay without a delay and report it as an adaptation.

issues.title: Position and audience of the recall questions are not stated
issues.reason: The recall questions are in the appendix and the footnote says a three-question battery was used, but the paper does not say where in the survey they came, and the control group was not asked the second and third questions.
issues.impact: The recall check cannot be placed in the sequence; asking it before the outcome questions could change the outcomes.
issues.suggestedAction: Obtain the survey flow from the authors. The replay does not administer recall.

issues.title: Eligibility criteria are not reported
issues.reason: The paper describes the panel but gives no eligibility or exclusion rules (the supplement's reporting checklist points to pages 2-3, which do not list them).
issues.impact: Cannot confirm who could take part; the panel is treated as U.S. adults only as an approximation.
issues.suggestedAction: Ask the authors or YouGov for the eligibility rules.

issues.title: Respondents per condition are not reported
issues.reason: Only model Ns (987, 986, 764) and the 231 control respondents not asked the investigation question can be inferred; the sizes of the innuendo, denial and causal arms are not given.
issues.impact: Prevents checking IPW weights and per-arm power; the replay uses equal arm sizes.
issues.suggestedAction: Request cell sizes from the authors or the replication data.

issues.title: Standard error type is not stated
issues.reason: Table 2 reports standard errors in parentheses but does not say whether they are classical or robust.
issues.impact: The replay's tests may differ slightly in p-values from the paper's.
issues.suggestedAction: Check the replication data when posted.

issues.title: Block definition is inferred
issues.reason: The paper says respondents were block-randomized on their answer to the crooked question but does not list the blocks.
issues.impact: The four response options are assumed to be the blocks.

issues.title: Weights cannot be reproduced
issues.reason: YouGov survey weights and the block inverse probability weights depend on the panel and the realized assignment, which are not available.
issues.impact: The evaluation reports unweighted estimates, which the paper's appendix says are substantively identical to the weighted ones.
issues.suggestedAction: Decide whether to treat unweighted OLS as the comparison model (default).

issues.title: AI participant background is not specified
issues.reason: The sample is described as approximately representative of the U.S. population with 35% Democrats and 27% Republicans, but the paper reports no individual-level characteristics that a prompt could use.
issues.impact: Adding personas would be an unsourced choice; by default none is added.
issues.suggestedAction: Decide whether AI participants should be given demographic or partisan backgrounds, and label that choice as a researcher decision.

issues.title: Sample demographics are available only on request
issues.reason: Details of the sample's demographic make-up are said to be available upon request; only party identification percentages and unweighted balance tables are printed.
issues.impact: Cannot describe the original sample fully.
issues.suggestedAction: Request the details from the authors.

issues.title: Response rate and participant flow are not reported
issues.reason: The supplement's reporting checklist lists the response rate and CONSORT diagram as pending with YouGov.

issues.title: The senator is called Don Swensen in Table 1 and Dan Swensen in the appendix questions
issues.reason: Table 1 uses 'Don Swensen' while the appendix outcome and recall questions say 'Dan Swensen'.
issues.impact: The replay shows both spellings exactly as printed; the inconsistency may reflect a typo in one source.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm with the authors which spelling respondents saw in the questions.

issues.title: Order of the outcome questions differs between the text and the appendix
issues.reason: The text introduces favorability, then bribes, then the investigation question; the appendix shows favorability, investigation, then bribes, and puts the investigation question on its own page.
issues.impact: The replay follows the appendix order.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm the order with the authors.

issues.title: Numeric codes in the appendix response options
issues.reason: The appendix prints bracketed numbers after each option (e.g. 'Very favorable [6]'); it is not stated whether respondents saw them or they are coding only.
issues.impact: The replay shows the labels only and scores them with the printed codes.
